# India’s EV Battery Ambitions: Access to Technology Matters More Than Factory Announcements

India has made a substantial push to build a domestic electric vehicle (EV) battery industry. Government incentives, investments by large conglomerates and plans for gigafactories have all pointed towards a greater role for Indian manufacturers in the battery supply chain.

Yet, the gap between announced capacity and operational production remains significant.

The central challenge is not simply building factories. It is acquiring the manufacturing expertise, process knowledge and material capabilities required to produce battery cells consistently, efficiently and at scale. China’s dominance in these areas has made that challenge considerably harder for Indian companies.

Recent developments involving JSW, Tata, Reliance and Ola illustrate the different approaches businesses are taking to overcome this constraint. They also raise a broader question: can India develop a competitive battery manufacturing industry when access to some of the most advanced technology remains difficult?

### 1. The gap between policy ambition and actual production

India’s Advanced Chemistry Cell production-linked incentive (PLI) scheme was designed to accelerate domestic battery manufacturing. With an outlay of ₹18,100 crore, the programme targets 50 GWh of battery-cell capacity. Of this, 40 GWh had been awarded, while the remaining 10 GWh was being tendered, according to the source document.

However, as of June 2026, only 1.4 GWh of capacity was operational, entirely attributable to Ola.

The numbers highlight a critical distinction between investment commitments and manufacturing capability.

A factory announcement, land acquisition or equipment installation does not necessarily translate into commercial-scale production. Battery manufacturing requires companies to develop processes that deliver consistent quality, long operating life and competitive costs across millions of cells.

That capability is built through repeated production runs, quality-control improvements and the reduction of manufacturing waste. It takes time to develop, even when the underlying technology is available.

The PLI scheme can encourage investment in capacity. But the operational progress described in the source suggests that incentives alone cannot resolve the technology and execution challenges facing the industry.

### 2. China’s advantage extends beyond battery-cell production

China’s position in the battery supply chain helps explain why Indian manufacturers are struggling to move from assembly to cell production.

According to the source document, China accounts for roughly 80% of global battery-cell production and more than 90% of LFP cathode material production

The advantage is not limited to possessing patents or technical manuals. It also reflects years of accumulated experience in operating production lines, managing quality and improving manufacturing yields.

This distinction is particularly important for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries. A company may obtain a licence to manufacture a cell, but that licence does not automatically transfer the practical knowledge required to make the process work reliably.

This practical expertise is often described as tacit knowledge. It develops through experience on the factory floor, troubleshooting production problems and training employees to operate equipment and maintain quality standards.

The implications are significant. Even if an Indian company secures the right to use a technology, it may still need substantial assistance from its technology partner before it can manufacture cells independently and efficiently.

India’s challenge, therefore, is not just technology acquisition. It is technology absorption.

### 3. Export restrictions and engineer mobility complicate technology transfer

The source identifies two additional constraints: Chinese restrictions on advanced manufacturing know-how and difficulties in bringing Chinese engineers to India.

In July 2025, China added certain aspects of LFP cathode-manufacturing technology to its restricted-export list. Some advanced know-how consequently required government approval before it could be transferred abroad, while less-advanced technologies remained outside those restrictions.

China subsequently announced broader controls across industries in October 2025 and suspended those broader rules in November. However, the July restrictions remained in place, according to the document.

The consequences extend beyond the licensing agreement itself.

In the case of Amara Raja’s arrangement with Gotion, Chinese engineers were expected to help install machinery, establish quality-control processes and train Indian employees. Difficulties in securing their participation reportedly hindered the transfer of manufacturing expertise.

There is also a commercial tension inherent in technology licensing. A company transferring its technology may gain access to a new market, but it also risks creating a future competitor. The source notes that this can limit the incentive to transfer knowledge beyond what is necessary to operate a factory.

India’s own scrutiny of Chinese investments adds another layer of complexity. The result is a difficult combination: Indian companies want to reduce dependence on imported batteries, but obtaining the technology needed to manufacture those batteries domestically can itself depend on cross-border commercial and geopolitical relationships.

### 4. Four companies, four different approaches

The most revealing aspect of India’s battery industry is how differently major companies are responding to the same underlying problem.

### A. JSW: From licensing to building its own expertise

JSW paused its battery-cell gigafactory plans on 26 August 2026 after struggling to secure a Chinese LFP technology partner. Four weeks later, it launched electric trucks and buses from a Maharashtra plant with annual production capacity of 15,000 vehicles. The vehicles are engineered in India, and their battery packs are assembled locally, but the cells are sourced externally.

On 28 September, JSW committed more than ₹800 crore to a battery research centre with COEP Technological University in Pune. The centre will work on lithium-ion and sodium-ion cells.

What it signals: JSW is pursuing a longer-term route towards developing its own capabilities while continuing with activities it can already execute domestically. Research investment, however, should not be confused with near-term commercial cell production.

### B. Tata: Different strategies for different chemistries

Agratas is building a 20 GWh battery-cell factory in Sanand, Gujarat. Production equipment began arriving in September 2026, and cell production is expected to start in 2027.

For NMC batteries, Agratas has licensed technology from AESC Apollo. For LFP batteries, it has been unable to secure a Chinese licensing partner and is developing the manufacturing process itself. The terms of the NMC arrangement are not public, so the degree of long-term technological independence it will provide remains unclear.

What it signals: Tata is using a mixed strategy rather than relying on one route for every battery chemistry. The key test will be whether the factory achieves production at scale and how much independent capability Agratas develops over time.

### C. Reliance: Acquiring intellectual property

Reliance has pursued technology ownership through acquisitions. It acquired almost all of Lithium Werks in March 2022 for approximately US$61 million, gaining a portfolio of 219 LFP patents, a manufacturing facility in China, existing employees and accumulated process technology. It had also agreed to acquire sodium-ion specialist Faradion in 2021 for approximately £100 million.

Yet, according to the source, Reliance subsequently explored an LFP technology-licensing arrangement with China’s Hithium. Those discussions reportedly stalled, and its cell-making plans were paused. Reliance has stated that its battery project is progressing on schedule, with its FY26 annual report describing the Jamnagar factory as nearing completion and planning 40 GWh of capacity.

What it signals: Acquiring patents and technology assets may strengthen a company's position, but it does not necessarily eliminate the need for further technical partnerships or continuing development. The precise technology underpinning Reliance’s planned cells remains unclear from the available information.

### D. Ola: Developing cells in-house

Ola has taken the route of developing cells internally. Its 4680 NMC cell is already used in its scooters, while its newer 46100 LFP cell has received BIS certification.

This represents progress beyond battery-pack assembly. However, Ola still imports key active materials, including cathode and anode materials.

What it signals: In-house cell development can reduce dependence on external cell suppliers, but it does not automatically create a fully domestic battery supply chain. Material sourcing remains an important part of the equation.

These strategies are not directly interchangeable. Licensing can accelerate entry into manufacturing, research can build proprietary knowledge, acquisitions can provide access to intellectual property, and in-house development can improve control over technology. Each approach has a different path to execution, and the source does not establish which will ultimately prove most successful.

### 5. The value chain matters as much as the factory

The battery supply chain is often discussed as though manufacturing a battery pack and manufacturing a battery cell are equivalent capabilities. They are not.

Indian companies such as Tata, Mahindra and Ather already assemble battery packs using cells sourced from elsewhere. Cell manufacturing is a more demanding activity because it requires consistent production quality, process optimisation and control over manufacturing yields.

The next layer is materials. Even companies that develop their own cells can remain dependent on imported inputs.

Ola illustrates this distinction: it has developed battery cells but continues to import key active materials. Reliance’s acquisitions illustrate a different route towards gaining access to technology, while JSW’s plans highlight the importance of research and process development.

The broader lesson is that domestic capability should be assessed across multiple stages:

* Battery-pack assembly: Can the company integrate cells, cooling systems, electronics and software?
* Cell manufacturing: Can it manufacture cells consistently and economically at scale?
* Technology ownership: Can it develop or control the processes required for its chosen battery chemistry?
* Material availability: Can it secure the critical inputs required for production?

Progress at one stage does not necessarily mean independence across the entire chain.

### 6. What this means for investors and businesses

For investors evaluating India's battery-manufacturing opportunity, the source points to several considerations that go beyond announced capacity.

First, assess operational progress rather than headline capacity. The gap between the PLI target of 50 GWh and the 1.4 GWh operational as of June 2026 demonstrates why announced capacity should not be treated as equivalent to commercial output.

Second, examine the depth of technology access. A licence may establish the right to use a process, but investors also need to understand whether the manufacturer can operate it independently, troubleshoot problems and improve production performance.

Third, distinguish between technological independence and supply-chain independence. Developing cells internally is meaningful progress, but imported active materials can still leave manufacturers exposed to external suppliers.

Fourth, evaluate the time horizon of research-led strategies. JSW’s investment of more than ₹800 crore in battery research represents a commitment to building capabilities. Its commercial impact, however, will depend on the results of that research and the company's ability to translate them into production.

Finally, partnerships and acquisitions need to be assessed on their actual contribution to manufacturing capability. Ownership of patents, access to a production facility or an agreement with a technology provider is not, by itself, proof of scalable and competitive output.

These considerations are particularly relevant when comparing businesses that operate at different stages of the battery value chain.

### 7. What to watch next

Three developments will help determine how quickly India’s domestic battery-cell industry progresses.

* Tata Agratas: Its Sanand factory is expected to begin cell production in 2027. Its commissioning and subsequent production progress will be an important test of India's ability to establish large-scale cell manufacturing.
* JSW’s research centre: The work on lithium-ion and sodium-ion technologies will offer an indication of whether domestic research can gradually reduce reliance on external technology providers. The commercial timeline remains uncertain.
* Ola’s manufacturing scale-up: Its experience will help illustrate whether in-house cell development can translate into sustained production at scale, while also showing the extent to which imported materials remain necessary.

Maruti offers a contrasting model. It imports the complete battery pack for its e-Vitara from BYD, avoiding the immediate need to develop cells or packs internally but retaining dependence on an external supplier.

The contrast is important: companies can participate in the EV market without controlling battery-cell technology, but the degree of control over costs, supply and manufacturing capabilities will differ depending on the chosen strategy.

### Conclusion: Building factories is only the first step

India’s battery-manufacturing ambitions are not held back by a single obstacle. The challenge combines the complexity of cell production, the difficulty of transferring practical manufacturing knowledge, restrictions on access to advanced technology and continuing dependence on imported materials.

JSW, Tata, Reliance and Ola are responding through different combinations of partnerships, acquisitions, research and in-house development. None of the strategies described in the source eliminates every constraint.

The next phase of the industry will therefore be judged less by how many gigafactories are announced and more by how many can produce cells reliably, at scale, and with progressively greater control over their underlying technology.

For India, the decisive milestone is not simply domestic battery production. It is the ability to build and sustain the expertise that makes that production commercially viable.

The EV market in India could represent an INR 5,000 Cr opportunity by 2025

Battery swapping and interoperability can play a vital role as they help build the supply chain network to boost EV adoption, which in turn will lead to a faster transition

It is vital to establish sustainable business models that can be leveraged to shift this upfront cost to the cost of operating an EV

Electric vehicles are becoming more prominent in today’s time, especially with the increasing use case in commercial vehicle space. In fact, according to Avendus Capital, the EVs in India could represent an INR 5,000 Cr opportunity by 2025. Many industry manufacturers and solution providers are working on the measures to make electric vehicles more affordable, easy to charge and economical to operate. One such technology that gives all these benefits to fleet operators is battery swapping. 

Battery swapping technology helps the user replace the depleted EV battery with a fully charged one.  A swapping station at any particular location generally comprises multiple batteries getting charged simultaneously. All it takes is for an EV user to locate a swapping station, replace the depleting battery with a charged one, put the empty battery on charge and go to work. 

Battery swapping technology has opened up quite a few opportunities for fleet owners who have range anxiety. Range anxiety refers to the fear an EV driver feels when the battery charge is low and the usual sources of electricity are unavailable.  

Apart from reducing the driver’s range anxiety, battery leasing can help EV consumers to save on the cost of purchasing a battery. It consumes minimum time and requires minimum infrastructure to charge at a battery station which could otherwise end up taking hours. 

## **A Positive Step But More Needs To Be Done**

With more than 12 Mn tonnes of lithium-ion batteries set to retire by 2030, the reliance on raw materials such as lithium, nickel and cobalt will only increase. At the end of their lives, batteries also create a lot of electronic waste. This will have a massive environmental effect. 

Many industry players are working on how to discard dead batteries and extract valuable metals at scale to keep materials in circulation and reduce reliance on mining. Though in my opinion, the industry should focus on a better solution to keep the battery in use for longer in alternative sectors.

Battery cost currently constitutes about 40-70% of the upfront cost for an electric vehicle. If these batteries are decoupled and sold separately, it can help shift the upfront cost to the energy operator’s network. This would essentially translate to shifting the cost of ownership to operations. Battery swapping and interoperability can play a vital role in this as they help build the supply chain network to boost EV adoption, which in turn will lead to a faster transition.

## **Aggressive Roadmap To Adopt Swapping**

Modern mobility solutions have two agendas — technology transition and mobility as a function. To change consumer behaviours and fundamentally change the ecosystem, we need to focus on an aggressive target with a proper roadmap for battery swapping. 

* **Use Standard Battery Technology**: Standardisation of the batter design is the answer to making battery switching easier. Whether it is a standard pack size, cavity, electric power control unit, or output performance per unit, these innovations serve as catalysts for achieving economies of scale more quickly.
* **Recycling Of EV Batteries:**Battery recycling offers a huge opportunity for the Indian market. When  EV batteries are built with a recycle-friendly design kept in mind, it will encourage the practice of repurposing. Additionally, if the manufacturers are encouraged to use recycled materials to make the batteries, it will eliminate sourcing. This will ultimately lead to reduced vehicular unit costs.
* **Battery-As-A-Service (BaaS):**Battery needs to be treated as a service segment such as LPG or other functional batteries. It is necessary to extend the incentives to battery-unit to subsidise per-kilometre operations rather than the purchase cost. The gross-cost financing models, along with the standard operating procedure for energy operators can help explore financially viable solutions.
* **Subscription Model Of Battery Swapping:** BaaS can be available to users at a subscription model to gain the trust of the users and to boost confidence in availability.
* **Building Co-Reliance:**It is important to identify the value-chain propositionsfor users, drivers, energy operators, urban local bodies and financing institutions in the swapping of EV batteries. Additionally, startups and big EV manufacturers should also focus on the inventory of previous existing modes, the infrastructure of land, space for parking, and spaces for charging infrastructure, among others.
* **Deploy Intelligent Transport Systems Technology:  The usage and promotion of** database based digital applications would aid in the human-to-machine and machine-to-machine interface. This would help increase EV and battery swapping station usage and traction. All the while ensuring efficient operations, safety detection, seamless delivery, and improved convenience in the EV ecosystem.

## **Challenges And The Way Through**

In the past few years, the global EV space has seen increased traction. This is despite the fact that the upfront costs of an EV are much higher than its Internal Combustion Engine (ICE) counterpart, with the battery pack making up at least half the cost.

To combat this, many manufacturers are offering batteries separately from a vehicle. In this case, a fleet owner can buy vehicles without batteries and utilise battery swapping to power their vehicles, reducing the initial cost.

Another major hindrance to purchasing an EV remains the range anxiety that the consumer suffers. Compared to petrol or diesel stations, EV charging facilities are hard to come by, which raises the range anxiety even more, especially when travelling long distances. The most efficient charger will replenish at most 80% of the battery in almost an hour.  That’s quite a considerable time taking into account that fuel pumps can fill up a tank in 5 minutes. In the case of a swapping station, one can simply locate a station and go and replace the empty battery with a new one.

In a bid to promote this practice, the government announced a battery swapping policy earlier this year. The policy mainly targets the battery swap services for three-wheeled auto-rickshaws and two-wheelers. Under the policy, EV consumers will get incentives of up to 20% on the subscription or lease cost of the battery. 

With the battery swapping technology still not being commonplace in the Indian market, there is a prevalence of charging stations. Though, the way ahead has to be focused on the creation of a robust swappable battery network. This network will mirror the existing network of fuelling stations to facilitate seamless operations. 

Private sector investment can be leveraged for operations of the supply chain networks and sustenance of energy operators. In this way, the battery swapping and network of energy operators become a service segment. The availability and connectivity of this energy infrastructure are critical to the operation of these exchanging stations. So, it is vital to establish sustainable business models that can be leveraged to shift this upfront cost to the cost of operating an EV.

# Electric Vehicles Sector in India

Last updated: September 29, 2026

## About Electric Vehicles sector in India

The Electric Vehicles sector in India comprises 2.85K companies, including 523 funded companies having collectively raised $10.7B in venture capital money and private equity. Out of these, 136 are Series A+ funded, and 2 have achieved unicorn status.

Electric Vehicles sector in India has seen 23 acquisitions and 19 IPOs.

This sector includes companies which help technology advancement in electric vehicle industry.

Electric Vehicles sector is also known as Green Vehicles or Electric Mobility.

Developers and manufacturers of electric vehicles (passenger and commercial vehicles including cars, trucks, buses, scooters, motorcycles, bicycles and personal transport equipment, marine vehicles, aerial vehicles, rail solutions, and off-highway vehicles which are used for construction, mining, farming, forklifts, etc. ), developers of charging infrastructure to support the electric vehicles and technology developers focusing on improving the components (Electric Drive Systems, Batteries, etc.) of electric vehicles. Also, includes online-first companies providing electric vehicle sharing and rental solutions resulting in increased adoption of electric vehicles. Sellers of EVs through retail and marketplace model are also covered. Traditional automakers such as Toyota, Renault-Nissan, General Motors, BMW, Mitsubishi, Ford, etc. which also develop electric vehicles. Also, excludes conglomerates like Panasonic, LG Chem, and Samsung which are leading battery manufacturers. Manufacturers and Ecommerce platforms selling Electric Mobility Aids are also excluded.

The Indian automobile industry is the fifth largest in the world, with a goal of becoming the third largest by 2030. India’s EV sector is rapidly expanding. The country has the world’s largest untapped market for electric vehicles, particularly in the two-wheeler segment. 

## **Government’s Push Towards Clean Mobility**

The Central Government is also prioritising the transition to clean mobility with recent moves to make electric two-wheelers more affordable under the FAME II scheme as of November 2021. 4.75 Lakh electric vehicles (EVs) have been registered and sold under this scheme.

Several approvals were granted under the FAME II scheme of the Indian EV policy. This includes approximately 6,315 electrical buses and 2,877 EV charging stations costing approximately $66.63 Mn in 68 cities across India, and 1,576 charging stations costing approximately $14.39 Mn across various expressways and highways. 

A number of production-related incentive schemes are now in place to support the goals of greater adoption of electric mobility as a mode of transportation. The government can achieve this goal if it is willing to incentivise and make new investments in developing indigenous supply chains for key technologies and products. 

Concerns about specific challenges related to inadequate supply chains, certain government policies, consumer behaviour, and proper EV charging infrastructure accompany the growth forecast. These obstacles must be considered when developing an appropriate India market entry strategy. 

This massive electric vehicle sector in India will take some time to develop. The automobile industry believes that India will follow in the low-carbon footsteps of many large developed countries. Every major automobile manufacturer intends to enter the EV market. Even though some domestic EV startups and OEMs already have EVs in their portfolio, other OEMs are all testing and planning to launch their own EVs within the next few years. 

While each of these manufacturers recognises the importance of EV mass market prospects, the government’s policy push has led them to take concrete steps that will make electric vehicles appealing. These OEMs, however, face a few challenges: 

### **Range Anxiety**

Range anxiety is the concern of an electric vehicle user about the number of kilometres an EV will travel, or how long the battery of the electric scooter will last. It is not possible to travel long distances on a single charge with the current battery technology installed in electric vehicles. 

### **Cost Of The Battery**

The battery and power electronics account for nearly two-thirds of the cost of an EV. Nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) and lithium-ion (LiON) are the most commonly used battery materials in the EV segment. Many factors, including gaps in the demand-supply chain, uneconomically low volumes, and so on, can contribute to the high cost of manufacturing EVs. The cost of an electric vehicle’s battery, power electronics, and motors can be six to seven times that of an IC engine. This has an additional impact on the ex-showroom price. 

We have seen new battery manufacturing capacities emerge in India over the last few years. The localisation push of these battery manufacturing can help to lower the costs of EVs. A battery manufacturing plant can produce up to 8 GWh of electricity. Localisation benefits can only be realised in the long run, with significant penetration and volumes of EVs. 

### **Supply Chain Problems**

Due to the scarcity of Lithium-ion, EV battery manufacturing in India is still heavily reliant on imports, which serves as a major impediment for companies looking to invest in India’s EV industry. Many startups are attempting to acquire stakes in overseas resources and are relocating more raw material manufacturing units to India. The Indian EV sector’s battery manufacturing capacity still requires proper and adequate planning. 

The industry also requires joint ventures to help it acquire sufficient lithium-ion battery resources. Foreign organisations are increasingly turning to consulting firms to assist them in assessing technology and industry trends in the EV sector and offering comprehensive business opportunities in India that will assist them in achieving profitable long-term gains.

### **Charging Infrastructure**

Consumers and fleets considering all-electric vehicles require charging stations, which are referred to as electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE). To address this issue, we must first charge at home or in fleet facilities. Charging stations in workplaces and public places can help to increase market acceptance. 

### **Lack Of Service Options**

Most of us have experienced a vehicle breakdown at some point in our lives. The problem is usually resolved due to the abundance of skilled/unskilled auto service technicians. With the growth of Indian OEMs and the EV segment in the country, there is a need for retraining repair professionals or finding newly trained EV workers. 

An electric vehicle has fewer moving parts than an ICE vehicle, but the technology is unknown to our informal service network. This causes anxiety among EV owners, who are constantly concerned about becoming stranded in the middle of nowhere. Even today, many auto OEMs have extensive service and dealer networks throughout India, but their EV service network has yet to mature significantly. 

The electric vehicle industry and OEMs in India are still in their infancy, but they are growing quickly. To keep up with this pace, we need EV infrastructure requirements that will support EV demand. Despite these obstacles, Indian OEMs and the electric vehicle industry have enormous potential to reduce carbon footprints and provide affordable vehicles. 

In the future, emobility will be essential for survival in India. So, rather than avoiding change, it is always preferable to plan how it will occur. An integrated EV policy for India’s future mobility, with a focus on zero-carbon emission mobility, is urgently needed. The future of electric mobility and the expansion of Indian OEMs, is here to stay, evolve, and broaden its reach.
